query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a thin refractory high‐entropy alloy interlayer at the W–Cu interface will suppress phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving the composite’s thermal conductivity under heat‐transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: W–Cu composite with either discrete W particles or an interconnected W ligament network in a Cu matrix that is prone to interphase diffusion and void formation at the W–Cu boundary.
generation.intervention: Introduce a uniform, thin coating of a refractory high-entropy alloy (for example, a composition similar to (CrFeTiTa)70W30) at the W–Cu interfaces during processing.
generation.conditions: Processing under controlled sintering temperatures (below the threshold for undesirable phase growth) and service conditions that simulate joint operation between W-based plasma-facing components and Cu-based cooling channels, including high thermal flux and irradiation exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: The high-entropy interlayer serves as a diffusion barrier, reducing intermixing between W and Cu and accommodating thermal expansion mismatches that otherwise provoke void formation.
generation.mechanism: By limiting interdiffusion and mitigating the stress accumulation at the interface, the interlayer prevents phase separation and void formation. This structural stabilization is expected to preserve the integrity of the W/Cu contact, maintaining a continuous heat-path and enhancing overall thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated composite will exhibit fewer interfacial voids and a more stable phase distribution with a correspondingly higher thermal conductivity compared to the untreated composite under equivalent high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated W–Cu composite that typically develops interfacial voids and phase separation under the same conditions, leading to reduced thermal conductivity.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for processing and operational temperatures that do not exceed the stability limits of the chosen high-entropy alloy, and at irradiation fluences similar to those used in experimental reactor-relevant tests. Its effectiveness may diminish if processing temperatures or irradiation doses far exceed these limits.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimum thickness and uniformity of the interlayer and how the high-entropy alloy will behave over very long service durations under simultaneous thermal and irradiation stresses.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one set of W–Cu composites with the high-entropy interlayer applied during processing and a control set without the interlayer. Subject both sets to identical sintering conditions followed by simulated operational conditions that include high thermal flux and irradiation exposures representative of plasma-facing joint environments.
measurements: Thermal conductivity (via steady-state or laser flash analysis)
Microstructural analysis (using SEM/TEM to assess interfacial continuity and void presence)
Phase analysis (using XRD or similar techniques)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy interlayer samples do not display a statistically significant decrease in phase separation and interfacial void formation, or if their thermal conductivity is not reliably higher than that of the control samples under the test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractNuclear fusion is a promising energy source. The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor aims to study the feasibility of tokamak-type reactors and test technologies and materials for commercial use. One major challenge is developing materials for the reactor’s divertor, which supports high thermal flux. Tungsten was chosen as the plasma-facing material, while a CuCrZr alloy will be used in the cooling pipes. However, the gradient between the working temperatures of these materials requires the use of a thermal barrier interlayer between them. To this end, refractory high-entropy (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys were prepared by mechanical alloying and sintering, and their thermal and irradiation resistance was evaluated. Both alloys showed phase growth after annealing at 1100 °C for 8 days, being more pronounced for higher temperatures (1300 °C and 1500 °C). The VFeTiTaW alloy presented greater phase growth, suggesting lower microstructural stability, however, no new phases were formed.
